chunks: I said to Abu Ibrahim (peace be upon him): 'A man who has a slave girl — does she make him muhsan (married/protected)?' Then he said: 'Yes, but rather it is on the basis of needlessness (of sexual satisfaction).'
He said: I said: 'And the woman of temporary marriage (mut'a)?' He said: Then he said: 'No, that (ihsan) is conditional upon that which is permanent (i.e., permanent marriage).'
He said: I said: 'But if he claims that he had not had intercourse with her?' He said: Then he said: 'He will not be believed, and rather that (hadd penalty) is imposed upon him because he owns her.'

key_terms.أَتُحْصِنُهُ: Does she make him muhsan? — the technical legal question of whether a relationship confers the married status requiring rajm if adultery is committed
key_terms.الشَّيْءُ الدَّائِمُ: The permanent thing — permanent (non-temporary) marriage, the only union that confers muhsan status according to this ruling
key_terms.الِاسْتِغْنَاءُ: Needlessness/sufficiency — the legal rationale that ownership of a slave girl gives the man access to lawful intercourse, making him 'needless' of illicit relations
key_terms.الْمُتْعَةُ: Mut'a — temporary marriage (nikah al-mut'a), a time-limited marriage contract recognized in Shia law
key_terms.يُوجَبُ ذَلِكَ عَلَيْهِ: That is imposed upon him — the hadd punishment (rajm) is applicable, since legal ownership is sufficient basis regardless of the man's claim

ai.seo_question: Does owning a slave girl or temporary marriage (mut'a) confer muhsan status in Shia Islamic law?
ai.summary: Imam Musa al-Kadhim (AS) rules on three jurisprudential questions regarding the concept of ihsan — the marital status that makes adultery punishable by rajm (stoning). First, ownership of a slave girl does confer ihsan status, justified on the basis that ownership provides sexual needlessness. Second, a temporary marriage (mut'a) does not confer ihsan, because ihsan requires a permanent union. Third, if a man claims he never had intercourse with the slave girl he owns, his claim is not accepted in court, because ownership itself is the legal basis for imposing the hadd penalty. The hadith reflects early Shia fiqh discussions in the context of pre-modern Islamic family and property law.

en.hubeali:
Ali, from Muhammad Bin Isa, form Yunus, from Is’haq Bin Ammar who said, 
‘I said to Abu Ibrahim<sup>asws</sup> (7<sup>th</sup> Imam<sup>asws</sup>), ‘The man, there happens to be a slave girl for him, would that make him as married?’ So he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘Yes. But rather, he is upon an aspect of the needlessness’.
I said, ‘And the woman of temporary marriage?’ So he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘But rather, that (being married) is upon the thing permanent’.
